Softmax is not the production model.

It is one of the standard published architectures, measured against the market on the same races as every other report here. Nothing in it is a promotion decision, and the promotion gates it can and cannot satisfy are in the technical appendix.

How each evaluation year was fitted

The 2016 evaluation model was trained on the initial 2010-2015 set. Each later evaluation adds the preceding complete season, so the training window expands by one year; the 2026 model uses 2010-2025. Every evaluation year is fitted separately -- 11 fits in all -- and no evaluation year's outcomes appear in its own fit.

Deltas in this report use model_minus_market_log_loss: race_multinomial_log_loss, where negative is better. That is stated because three delta fields existed in this repository and they did not all point the same way.

Provenance -- the source commit, the config and data digests, the environment and every input this report read by content digest -- is in the technical appendix and in run_lock.json beside this file. Canonical publication fails without it.

Softmax is better than the market by 0.000992 race_multinomial_log_loss on 7,933 races. The direction holds in 7 of 11 evaluated years. Race by race it is ahead 51.7% of the time, which is the more honest figure: a mean delta can be carried by a few races. 13,793 bets were selected under the staking rules below, on retrospective odds that could not have been bet into.

Evaluation population and market reference

The market reference

Every metric below is reported beside the market's own implied probabilities on the same races, normalised within each race, and the delta is this model's race log loss minus the market's on the same races. One yardstick across every published report, so their headline numbers mean the same thing and can be read against one another. The market is a measurement, not a model this one is defined against.

The evaluation population

Every figure in this report covers the standardized evaluation window, which begins in 2016. One window for every published report, so their headline numbers are computed on the identical race keys and can be compared -- which is checked by digest before anything is published, not asserted in a footnote. 2015 is earlier than the window and is excluded from every evaluation figure below, including the bankroll paths. The feature-effect grid is the one exception, and says so where it appears: a learned response direction is a property of each year's fit rather than of the evaluation population.

The largest departure is the 0.000 to 0.010 bin, and every stage misses there: market 0.54, raw_utility 0.94, temperature 0.93, bagged 0.93. market is furthest from 1.0 at 0.54, meaning that bin won fewer races than it priced; raw_utility is closest at 0.94, so this bin is where the pipeline moves calibration most. On the market stage that bin holds 10,889 runners, the 6th smallest of 10 bins, so the departure is not a thin-bin artefact. Calibration in this bin does not improve monotonically through the pipeline: temperature reaches 0.93 and bagged falls back to 0.93, so that step gives back part of the correction rather than adding to it.

How often this model's first pick differs from the market's, and whether it is right when it does. This grid covers every year the run fitted, including any the evaluation population excludes. A learned response direction is a property of that year's fit rather than of the race population the headline metrics are computed on, and its per-feature mean is the stability table's tail_effect exactly -- so restricting one and not the other would have two parts of this report describe different populations. 14 of 28 features keep the same sign in every year they appear in. For the seven features that are constant within a race -- a racecourse, a surface -- the cell is the correction's magnitude and not its direction, because a race-constant feature cancels from every pairwise utility difference and has no direction to report. Which basis a row uses is in its tooltip and in the stability table's curve_basis column. A feature whose row changes colour is not necessarily broken: it may genuinely matter differently in different years. But its mean effect is then a summary of disagreeing years, and the mean is the least informative number about it.

Betting and bankroll analysis

Retrospective odds

Every stake, return and bankroll figure in this report is computed against historical result-page odds and official dividends. Those are not an executable pre-race price: they are the prices after the pool closed, and a bet placed at them could not have been placed. Nothing here establishes profitability. A profitability claim requires a locked model shadow-tested against timestamped pre-race odds snapshots.

Do not select a threshold from these returns.

Every year through 2026 has been used as development data in this repository: features were searched, architectures compared and thresholds inspected against these same seasons. The chronological split is real, so a test year is genuinely after its training rows, but no test year is unseen. Treat the forward figures as probability progress rather than as a locked out-of-sample result, and do not select a Kelly level or an edge threshold from this reused history. The confirmation step that this run cannot substitute for is a prospective shadow test against archived pre-race price snapshots.

Softmax is not the production model, and this is not a proposal to stake it.

A settled ledger measures what a probability was worth economically, which is a different question from which model should carry money. That decision is the production model's, and the comparison that would inform it is in the technical appendix rather than in this table.

Settlement by staking rule

RoleWhat it is for
Primarywhat an operator would run: sized for the rebate, and credited it.
Sizing referencethe same settlement, sized blind. It isolates sizing for the cliff from receiving the rebate -- this row and the primary settle identically and differ only in what the solver knew.
Settlement ablationblind sizing with the rebate not credited. It isolates the rebate's own contribution to the return.
Benchmarka fixed flat stake above an edge floor, sized from the opening bankroll and never resized. Not a Kelly fraction, so it belongs to no preset panel below -- and it has no ruin stop, so a model that finds edge in most races can stake more than the bankroll holds and finish below zero. That is the yardstick behaving as defined rather than a settlement error: it is here to show what indiscriminate staking on this model's edges would have done, which is why it is a benchmark and not a proposal.

The table below is ordered by that role rather than alphabetically, so the first Kelly rows are the ones an operator would run.

Flat stake@edge>=0.02 closed below zero.

The flat-stake benchmark is sized from the opening bankroll and never resized, so it has no ruin stop: a model that finds edge in most races stakes more than the bankroll holds. The closing figure is what that rule would have owed, not a bankroll that existed. Every Kelly rule here sizes from the running bankroll and cannot do this.

The check that matters most in this section: if the realised return in each edge bucket does not track the expected one, the edge estimate is wrong and every stake sized from it is wrong with it. The bucket counts are small enough that one winner moves a bucket, so read the pattern across buckets rather than any single number.

A negative-edge bucket appears only under rebate-aware sizing, and only at the larger fractions. That is the rule working as defined rather than a filter failing: the rebate is a cliff, so a runner whose own edge is negative can pay for itself by pushing the race's turnover over the threshold, and the stakes only get large enough for that at the higher fractions.

The 2016 evaluation model was trained on the initial 2010-2015 set. Each later evaluation adds the preceding complete season, so the training window expands by one year; the 2026 model uses 2010-2025. Every evaluation year is fitted separately -- 11 fits in all -- and no evaluation year's outcomes appear in its own fit. Each path is rebased on its own opening balance, so zero means break-even for every line from the same point. These curves are drawn from a bounded 1,000-point subsequence of up to 7,529 staked races, keeping each interval's highest and lowest balance so no peak or drawdown is smoothed away, and keeping the first and last points exactly. Every figure in the tables is computed from the full settlement, and the complete per-race path is in <code>race_paths.parquet</code>. Where a year is excluded, a continuous path opens at the balance the bank held when the kept years begin and an annual-reset path opens at the declared bankroll, so the two show different opening figures for the same rule. Rebate policy: 10% of the race net loss, once that loss reaches HK$10,000, as a cliff. Flat staking is omitted from these panels. Its stake is a fixed amount per bet and this settlement never halts on ruin, so its path can pass below zero -- a measure of how badly a rule loses rather than a balance an account could hold. It is also not a Kelly fraction, so it belongs to no preset. Its settlement is in the strategy table above. annual-reset re-settlement of continuous-path decisions: the same stakes, compounded from the declared opening balance at the start of each test year. Not an annual-reset sizing simulation -- stakes are not re-solved from reset capital, and doing so would change which bets are placed rather than only how they compound. Each bankroll scenario below is solved from its own opening balance, sequentially by race, because the rebate threshold is a fixed dollar amount and the fraction the solver sees therefore changes with the bank. The larger scenario is not the smaller one's stakes scaled up. 2015 is excluded from every path below. That year's utility scale fell back to its theoretical value rather than being fitted, so its stakes are not comparable with the rest.

Winners drawn from the model's own probabilities. 9 of 53 settled series shown, filtered to model view softmax_bagged.

One simulation was declined rather than approximated

Refusals are recorded rather than omitted, so a reader can see the strategy was considered and declined. Rebate-aware sizing cannot reuse stale bankroll-dependent fractions on a divergent path.

The realised path, the day-block bootstrap and the model-assumed MC answer different questions and must not be shown as one uncertainty band.

What a simulation cannot tell you

The model-assumed simulation draws winners from the model's own probabilities. If those probabilities are wrong the simulation is confidently wrong in the same direction, so it bounds sampling risk and says nothing about model risk.

The generating source tree was dirty

This run's provenance records uncommitted changes, so the commit named above does not fully describe the code that produced these numbers. Treat the figures as indicative until the report is regenerated from a clean tree.

Every input this report read is listed in run_lock.json by content digest, together with the lock digest of the run that produced them -- which is what chains a published figure back through the report to the fit and from there to the feature table's own digest.

Limitations and the retrospective-odds warning

Retrospective odds, restated

Every stake, return and bankroll figure in this report is computed against historical result-page odds and official dividends. Those are not an executable pre-race price: they are the prices after the pool closed, and a bet placed at them could not have been placed. Nothing here establishes profitability. A profitability claim requires a locked model shadow-tested against timestamped pre-race odds snapshots.

Restated at the end as well as beside the betting numbers, deliberately. It is the single most load-bearing caveat in this report and the one a reader skimming for a return figure is most likely to miss.

Every test year is also development data

Every year through 2026 has been used as development data in this repository: features were searched, architectures compared and thresholds inspected against these same seasons. The chronological split is real, so a test year is genuinely after its training rows, but no test year is unseen. Treat the forward figures as probability progress rather than as a locked out-of-sample result, and do not select a Kelly level or an edge threshold from this reused history. The confirmation step that this run cannot substitute for is a prospective shadow test against archived pre-race price snapshots.

What else this report does not establish

  • It measures Softmax against the market on the same races. It does not measure this model against the other published models except through that shared yardstick.
  • Its intervals condition on the fitted model, so they bound sampling risk and not model risk.
  • Every figure is out of sample in time but in sample in design: the feature set, the hyperparameters and the staking rules were all chosen with these years visible.
  • Nothing here is a shadow test. A profitability claim needs a locked model run forward against timestamped pre-race prices.
Unverified source state

This run recorded a dirty source tree, so its numbers cannot be reproduced from the named commit alone.
